title: Is using AI basically a death sentence for an indie project?
author: Frosty_Anteater_9832
selftext:
Hi fellow AI builders, I've been struggling with something for the last few months, especially with how heated the whole AI vs. anti-AI debate has become. I've always loved games and game development, but I do something completely different for a living. I tried learning to tools like Aseprite, Godot and Unity before, but the amount of skills involved always became a huge barrier. Then, around november/december, I started seriously experimenting with AI. At first it felt almost too easy: a few prompts and suddenly you have something vaguely resembling a game.

I was very very wrong.

As soon as I tried turning prototypes into an actual coherent game, I started dealing with bugs, broken interactions, mechanics that needed redesign and endless small fixes. Add a mechanic. Break three things. Fix them. Change your mind. Refactor. Repeat. If you're on this sub, you probably know the drill.

And weirdly enough, that's when I started enjoying it much more. AI saves me a huge amount of time and lets me overcome all the technical barriers (and errors in particular) that surely would have stopped me otherwise. But, based on this little experience, it definitely is not "write three big prompts and ship a game." Since December I've been designing mechanics, testing prototypes, sketching characters, using AI for parts of the art and code, then manually editing, fixing and iterating on the results. I'm now roughly halfway to something I'd actually call a playable demo. And that's where some sort of "crisis" started.

I asked myself: Did I actually make this game? I think I did.

I couldn't recreate most of the code from scratch without AI. But I designed the mechanics, decided how systems should interact, tested everything, rejected bad solutions, changed things and kept iterating and innovating until they worked and feel fun. The same applies to the art. Some sprites started from my sketches, some from AI generations, and I've spent a ridiculous amount of time fixing pixel art manually in Aseprite.

So no, this isn't a traditionally hand-coded and hand-pixelled game. But it's also not a bunch of untouched AI outputs thrown together in an engine. And that's my real problem. I'm worried that the moment people see the text: "AI was used," none of that will matter. The project will simply get labelled AI slop regardless of how much work, design and iteration went into it and that has honestly started hurting my motivation.

When I began getting results I was proud of, I imagined eventually releasing the game and maybe selling it for a few bucks. Not because I expect some huge indie success, but because I loved the idea that people might actually play this world I've been building and maybe consider it worth paying a small amount for.

Now I'm wondering whether charging money makes the whole AI issue much worse: "Here's this game I made with AI, it's free." vs. "Here's this game I made with AI, it's €5." For some reason, in my head, the second one seems to cross a completely different line for a lot of people.

I'm not looking for "ignore the haters" comments, i'm genuinely looking for your thoughts on the matter, trying to figure out what to do with the project once the demo is ready.

TL;DR: I've spent months building a game with heavy AI assistance, but also a lot of manual design, editing, testing and iteration. I'm worried that releasing it, especially as a paid game, will automatically get it dismissed as AI slop and get ton of hate. If you were in my position, what would you actually do with the game?

comments.author: Perfson

I honestly believe that most people aren't against AI. They are against slop. If your game looks and sound like a slop, with low quality or uncanny assets, it's just gonna be instantly ignored/bombed.   
  
If your game is looking flawless despite heavy AI usage, well, I think only hardcore AI haters are gonna avoid/bomb it, rest gonna buy and enjoy it. I saw AI enhanced animation videos and people like: "Is this AI? o.o wow I'm AI hater, buuut...". So, just focus on making quality product.

And at that point, the limits of your imagination and how you articulate that to the world will be the deciding factor on who likes your game or not.

replies.author: foodeyemade
replies.body:
Realistically that's never happening with a game that isn't a direct clone of an existing one (at least not with llms).  Just getting the balance right and the moment to moment, short term, and long term gameplay all feeling satisfying and meshing well isn't something AI can really do. You have to playtest and tune extensively which is honestly half the work in making a great game.  
  
Generating all the assets and systems and having it all be perfectly cohesive is theoretically possible (although we are nowhere close), but actually one shotting a full ready to publish balanced game is never happening without an actual general AI.

replies.author: IAgreeGames
replies.body:
Yes, general AI, or long lived LLMs with multi-million token runs + persistent memory will probably be needed, but this just a when, not if.

I also agree that finding the right feel and balance of your game will become more of the job vs coding.

When playtesting your game becomes your job, then we've all made it. That what my job has mainly become, AI builds the majority of my apps, and I test them to make sure they meet requirements and to suss out any bugs.

VG's will go the same way. People will write code because they like to write code, and the appreciate the art of it, not because they like making video games.

comments.author: BadImpStudios
comments.body:
I’ve been spending quite a lot of time on this recently, particularly helping people work through game/design projects where AI is involved.

I’ve worked with hundreds of developers over the years through tutoring, development and consulting, and more recently I’ve been doing a lot more design consultation around AI-driven projects.

The biggest thing I’ve noticed is that people often don’t actually need more AI tools or another pile of generated ideas. They need someone to help untangle what they’re trying to build, challenge some of the assumptions, work out what’s actually worth pursuing, and turn the fuzzy idea into something concrete.

A few clients have come in with projects that were basically a cloud of features and possibilities, and after a consultation they’ve been able to move forward with a much more defined direction, clearer scope and actual next steps.

That side of the work has ended up being something I really enjoy as well — getting into the weeds of the idea rather than just saying “here are 47 things you could do with AI”.

If anyone here is working on something similar and feels a bit stuck, I’m open to consultations. Happy to have a look at what you’re building and help you properly pull it apart.

I did not mention in clearly this in my post but, unfortunately, i have no budget at the moment for this personal project, maybe in the future i will consider using it for something really specific and possibly with a low cost but thanks for sharing your experience and for proposing a consultation!

comments.author: CautiousCarry4209

There is a a difference between working together with the AI, and letting AI make the game for you. If you outsource everything to the AI things go fast but the quality will be generic and feel less human. I don't think AI ever will be able to make games of top quality because they can't relate to us a 100 %, a skilled human needs to be involved in the process.

What op is describing is AI assisted game development and I believe this will be the future, but many people are too negative to give it the benefit of the doubt. People will lose their job because of this technology but new ones will be created. If you are a composer now you can put your music into a interactive experience with the help of AI, if your a graphic designer now you can make your own game with your art in it, if your a coder now you can build intricate codes and get AI to help speed the process. 

Small indie teams, that did not have the resources will come up with great games because of AI. The bad games that take a week to make will eventually stop as people making them, realise there is no money to be made, also the AI business is heavily subsided by investor money, in a not too distant future prices of using their services will have to increase. Use the tools you have at your disposal, an engineer is not hated on becuses he uses an advanced program to calculate how to construct 300 m long bridge.

comments.author: CalebKious
comments.body:
I think you made the game.

I say that as someone who has gone pretty far down the AI-assisted development path. I run a solo software/game company, Bezhig LLC, and have used Codex heavily while building multiple games, including a released iOS/Android game and FateMMO, an MMORPG built on my own custom C++23 engine.

The distinction I think gets lost in the AI debate is between **authorship and implementation**.

If you decide what the game is, design its mechanics, determine how its systems interact, playtest it, recognize when something sucks, throw away bad implementations, change the art direction, rebalance progression, fix edge cases, and iterate until the experience matches what you had in your head, you’re doing game development.

AI doesn’t make those decisions for you.

I’ve actually found that the further a project gets beyond the prototype stage, the more obvious this becomes. You can tell Codex to implement a system and get something impressive surprisingly quickly. But now make that system coexist with 30 other systems. Make it persistent. Make it multiplayer. Handle disconnects. Handle malicious clients. Make the UI intuitive. Make it work on iOS and Android. Optimize it. Test it. Change the design six weeks later without breaking everything else.

Suddenly the prompt isn’t the product anymore. **Your decisions are.**

I’ve had AI write code that compiles perfectly and is completely wrong for the game. I’ve had generated art that looks great in isolation but doesn’t fit the visual language of everything around it. I’ve thrown away enormous amounts of generated work. Knowing *what should exist* and recognizing *what shouldn’t ship* are huge parts of authorship.

I also wouldn’t hide your AI use, but I wouldn’t make it the identity of the game either.

Don’t market it as **“THE AI-GENERATED GAME.”**

Market the game.

Show the combat. Show the characters. Show the world. Show whatever makes your game fun. If someone asks how you made it, tell them: you designed it, used AI extensively as part of your toolchain, manually edited assets, iterated in Aseprite, tested and redesigned mechanics, etc.

And yes, **I would charge for it if it’s worth €5.**

Customers aren’t paying you according to how many keystrokes you personally typed. They’re paying for the experience you’re offering them.

We don’t discount a game because the developer used Unity instead of writing a renderer. We don’t discount it because Photoshop has content-aware tools, because an engine generated a navmesh, because Blender calculated lighting, because a programmer used Stack Overflow, or because a studio bought assets instead of modeling every chair themselves.

AI is obviously a much more powerful abstraction than those examples, and there are legitimate ethical questions around particular models and training data. But I don’t think the logical conclusion is that anything touched by AI must therefore be free.

There **is** a real AI-slop problem. I’ve seen exactly what people are reacting to: someone generates a pile of inconsistent assets, has an LLM produce a generic game around them, does almost no editing or QA, and throws it onto a storefront hoping to make money.

The answer isn’t to avoid AI. The answer is to make something that very obviously isn’t slop.

Polish is probably your strongest defense.

If the animations are coherent, UI is deliberate, mechanics interact thoughtfully, progression feels good, bugs are handled, art has a consistent direction, sound design fits, controls feel good, and there are little details that exist because *you cared enough to put them there*, people can see the difference.

And you’re describing months of exactly that process.

One thing AI has taught me is that **making code cheaper doesn’t make taste, persistence, direction, or judgment irrelevant. It arguably makes them more important.** When everyone can generate 10 implementations, the valuable skill becomes knowing which implementation deserves to survive.

My own projects have reached scopes I simply could not have realistically attempted alone several years ago. FateMMO’s wider project has approached a million tracked lines across the engine, game, server, tests, tools, data and documentation, with thousands of tests and a custom editor, renderer, networking stack, database infrastructure, cross-platform clients, etc. I don’t pretend I manually typed every line. Codex has been an enormous force multiplier.

But Codex also didn’t wake up one morning and decide to build FateMMO.

I did.

I decided what it should be, what systems it needed, what wasn’t good enough, what needed rewriting, what the world should look like, and whether something was finally ready to ship.

From what you described, you’re doing the same thing.

Finish the demo. Put it in people’s hands. Don’t ask them whether they’re impressed that AI helped make it.

Ask them whether the game is **good**.

If the answer eventually becomes yes, charge the €5.

comments.author: DigitalDustChan
comments.body:
I think you could just as well say "is it really my game if someone else wrote the engine?" More lines of code probably go into the engine than into what you wrote, so couldn't you just call it "Unity with a skin"?

If you think about it that way then I think it becomes obvious that the person with the direction and drive to implement your vision is the person who created the game. If AI made the code then it was a tool that you used to implement. It wouldn't have made that code if you weren't there.

Remember Walt Disney? Did he make Mikey Mouse? The conscious is that he did, even though other artists actually drew 99% of the art. He had the vision and the authority to take credit, so he made it. Your case is the same.

replies.author: Frosty_Anteater_9832
replies.body:
Yeah, that's an interesting way of looking at it. You could make the same argument about developers who use free or purchased assets: they didn't create the art themselves, but we still generally consider them the creators of the game because they designed the mechanics, wrote the code, and put everything together.

That said, I think the AI issue goes deeper than that.

Walt Disney didn't personally draw Mickey Mouse, but Mickey was still created by human artists within a human creative process, with Disney heavily involved in the direction. With AI, part of that human creative chain can disappear entirely: the art, code, animation, etc. may be generated without another person actually doing that work.

So to me, the question isn't only "can I legitimately say I made the game?" I think it's also an ethical, political, and maybe even existential question about what happens when human creative labor is increasingly replaced by AI.

That doesn't make the authorship question unimportant, but I think the real issue goes beyond authorship alon

comments.author: Not_Allowed_to_Die
comments.body:
Ask yourself this, and you will have your answer. It's a simple question to answer only to yourself. 

If you did have a team of developers that you did all of this and told them what to do and how to make the game, would you still claim you made the game? All the AI did was fire these people, and replaced them. Now, do you feel you did enough work that if people did what the AI did, you could still claim you MADE it. Not that you came up with the ideas for it, but you told the AI the logical pathways needed in the programming and used it as a grunt doing the grunt work. Or, did you tell the AI your ideas, and it did all of the work? 

You don't have to answer this to anyone at all, but yourself. What everyone else thinks doesn't matter when it comes to the answer you hold inside. But you have to HONESTLY answer this to yourself and ask yourself as well, could I have learned to do more? Could I have profit shared and made a strong team, or was this enough? These are the questions every AI user needs to ask. If you answer it to yourself in shame, then fix that and make a team. If you answered it with you're okay with it, then do your path your way. But, don't expect anyone on either path to accept anything you do. It's up to you to create and see where the chips lay afterwards.

replies.author: Frosty_Anteater_9832
replies.body:
That's a really interesting perspective, and it's exactly part of why I made this post.

In my case, I can honestly say I wrote 0 lines of code, while I did and will make part of the art, animations and effects (still heavly involving AI). So yes, in a sense I'm closer to a game designer/director than someone who personally created every part of the game.

Where I slightly disagree is with the idea that AI simply "fired" the people who would have done that work. That makes sense for a studio with a budget. In my case, though, I was never realistically going to hire a team. This is a hobby project that I may pause or even abandon, and I don't feel comfortable asking other hobbyists to invest months or years into something I'm not sure I can finish myself.

So without AI, the alternative probably isn't "the same game made by humans." It's simply "this game doesn't exist."

And that's also why I'm unsure that releasing it for free completely solves the ethical question. The AI is still replacing work someone could theoretically have done, even if nobody was actually going to be hired.

Thanks anyway, I'll definitely keep your question in mind. I think it's a very useful point of view.
